body:
A public elliptic-curve key tells us the result of repeatedly adding a known point to itself. The secret is how many additions were made. Shor's algorithm can recover that number on a quantum computer. This paper asks what it would take to carry out the entire calculation on an error-corrected trapped-ion machine.

Compiled model · one attempt

The task is to recover \(d\) from the public points \(P\) and \(Q=[d]P\) on secp256k1. The estimate follows one key-recovery attempt from its arithmetic to its physical measurements.

19,397physical qubits
25.690days per attempt

The modeled attempt succeeds with probability 63.3% using heuristic classical recovery. Starting from the conservative Fourier bound gives 40.7%, assuming classical search resolves the omitted 48 bits. The success lesson explains how arithmetic errors and hardware survival enter those numbers.

The interesting question

Most of the arithmetic proceeds serially: one carry or one division step must finish before the next can use it. Speed therefore depends on making each logical operation fast and doing movement and cleanup during otherwise available time. The paper constructs a machine and schedule around that requirement.

From a hidden scalar to a measurement schedule

We begin by encoding the secret in a Fourier relation. Producing that relation requires a sequence of point additions. Each addition loads a known point from a classical table, updates the quantum accumulator, and clears its temporary information so interference is preserved.

Inside each addition, division is costly. A record of gcd reductions applies the needed inverse directly to the numerator and saves a separate inverse register. Short arithmetic saves more work. Random masks make its errors amenable to a per-input success bound.

Next we put those operations on the machine. The compiler moves registers while arithmetic proceeds; Clifford-frame clearing keeps later measurements accessible. Finally, four CCZ factories supply the states consumed by Toffoli gates. These steps turn a reversible algorithm into a timed measurement schedule.

Where the time goes

The chart below shows which parts of that schedule consume time. Every bar uses its measurement-layer count multiplied by 0.0294958 seconds, the common duration charged in the paper. Multiplication and lookup account for most of the result.

The complete schedule contains 40.42 million Toffoli injections and 75.25 million measurement layers. The first total counts a consumed resource. The second also includes movement, measurement, and cleanup, and is the quantity used to calculate runtime.

Choose a route

The introduction establishes the problem and units. The algorithm lesson begins the construction. The remaining pages follow the paper's sections and explain its borrowed methods where they enter; source coverage and Limitations collect the supporting record and unresolved questions.

title: Breaking 256-bit elliptic-curve signatures: a circuit-to-hardware study

body:
Two moduli, two jobs

Start with a known curve point \(P\), add it to itself a secret number \(d\) of times, and publish the resulting point \(Q\). Recovering \(d\) from \(P,Q\) is the elliptic-curve discrete-logarithm problem. This estimate follows one quantum attempt to recover that scalar.

For secp256k1, the points satisfy \[y^2=x^3+7\pmod p,\qquad p=2^{256}-2^{32}-977.\] The curve equation determines which coordinate pairs are allowed. The secret appears through group addition, \(Q=[d]P\), rather than through either coordinate alone.

Coordinates

Coordinate calculations use the prime \(p\): adding, multiplying, or dividing \(x,y\) means field arithmetic in \(\mathbb F_p\).

Scalars

Counting point multiples uses the order \(r\) of \(P\): after \(r\) additions the group returns to its identity, so the scalar \(d\) is defined modulo \(r\).

What a complete estimate connects

To estimate the machine, we must connect several descriptions. Reversible arithmetic specifies the desired logical operations. The compiler places their encoded qubits in code blocks and schedules compatible measurements. The architecture supplies the physical ions, checks, transport, and resource states that perform those measurements.

The missing unit is a measurement layer

A Toffoli count alone does not include all that work. Moving a register or clearing an ancilla can require a measurement even when no additional Toffoli state is consumed. The useful timing unit is therefore a scheduled measurement layer: operations that can run together on the specified device.

\[\underbrace{T}_{\text{runtime}}=\underbrace{D}_{\text{scheduled layers}}\;\underbrace{\tau}_{\text{seconds per layer}}.\]

The schedule has \(D=75{,}251{,}329\) layers. Charging each layer \(\tau=0.0294958\,\mathrm{s}\) gives 616.555 hours, or 25.690 days. The rest of the paper explains how the circuit, placement, and measurement protocol produce those two inputs to the runtime calculation.

The device being estimated

The calculation assumes the proposed trapped-ion device and its specified operation rates, including a two-qubit Pauli error scale of \(10^{-4}\). It assigns every logical measurement the CCZ-injection mean duration. The overview explains the design changes behind that duration and the corresponding footprint.

title: I. Introduction: what does a complete resource estimate count?

body:
Match the machine to a serial circuit

The arithmetic repeatedly consumes a Toffoli gate and waits for its result. That makes the latency of one logical operation central to the design. The paper combines a direct Toffoli resource, parallel measurements, and background correction clearing to shorten this repeated wait.

In the baseline Walking Cat implementation used for comparison, a Toffoli is assembled from seven T states. Each state supplies a non-Clifford T gate, \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), but the injections and their corrections also take time. Producing the resource the application needs directly removes that sequence.

Design choiceWhat changesWhy it helps
Direct CCZ statesOne three-qubit resource per ToffoliShorter injection sequence
Disjoint Pauli supportsThree joint parities measured togetherOne measurement layer
Idle frame clearingCorrect upcoming blocks in advanceLess blocking on the serial path
Integrated routingCompute while relocating registersFewer separate movement layers

Supply is only half the timing problem

Direct CCZ states remove a sequence of separate T injections. The factories must produce them at least as fast as the data can consume them.

Supply

Four factories together produce an accepted CCZ state in under 28 milliseconds on average, matching the application's demand.

Consumption

The application consumes at most one CCZ state in each charged layer of about 29.5 milliseconds.

The prepared state is \(|\mathrm{CCZ}\rangle=\mathrm{CCZ}|+\rangle^{\otimes3}\). Hadamards before and after its target turn CCZ into Toffoli. Injecting it quickly requires three measurements to use disjoint physical supports in each block. The support construction explains why logical commutation alone does not supply this parallelism.

Count capacity and workspace separately

Dense encoding supplies the workspace. Q102 is a \([[102,22,9]]\) code: 102 data ions encode 22 logical qubits at distance 9. Sixty-nine memory blocks provide 1,518 slots for the peak 1,457 logical qubits. Four more blocks clear accumulated Clifford corrections; the factories, cat states, and replacement ions complete the 19,397-ion total.

Approximation is a resource

The arithmetic also trades a controlled error probability for fewer gates. It truncates carries and phase comparisons, then randomizes the inputs relevant to their failure analysis. If ideal success is at least \(P_0\) and each input fails with probability at most \(p_f\) over that randomization, \[P_{\rm alg}\ge\bigl(\max\{0,\sqrt{P_0}-2p_f\}\bigr)^2,\qquad p_f\le0.03346.\]

The bound subtracts \(2p_f\) from success amplitude before squaring. Its proof includes wrong phases even when output integers are correct. The success lesson derives this step and explains why the per-input randomization matters.

The repeated unit

The repeated arithmetic unit is one point addition. Sixteen-bit windows, a direct first lookup, and omission of 48 bits for classical recovery leave 28 such additions. Each uses two in-place multiplication/division operations and three coordinate lookups, which account for most of the runtime.

The final probability

Finally, combine algorithmic success with modeled hardware survival. The heuristic classical-recovery branch gives 63.3%; the conservative Fourier branch gives 40.7% with search covering the shortened-register ambiguity. Appendix E keeps the footprint, time per attempt, and success calculation separate until this final combination.

title: II. Overview: connect circuits, schedules, and hardware

body:
What carries beyond this estimate

The estimate comes from matching the whole computation to its machine. Recorded gcd reductions reduce arithmetic storage, movement overlaps with the serial calculation, and direct CCZ preparation supplies the gate the application repeatedly consumes. Their combined effect appears in the 75.25-million-layer schedule and the resulting 25.690-day attempt.

Limitations

The estimate depends on a proposed device and several different sources of evidence. The following gaps identify the additional demonstrations or calculations needed to validate it end to end.

Assumption or gapDecisive next check
Full-device transport, timing, and swap-loss modelValidate long-duration behavior with a more detailed trap-and-loss model.
Independent hardware-failure categoriesModel correlated failures; compare the 26.46% product estimate with the 27.44% union bound.
Classical recovery after omitting 48 bitsSpecify search cutoffs and measure classical runtime. The main table charges the quantum schedule.
Internal compiler and noise simulationsRelease schedules, decoder settings, simulator inputs, and error samples for independent reproduction.

The 19,397-ion device is a proposed design. Its transport, loading, operation fidelities, and decoder behavior must hold over the attempt. Logical memory rates are extrapolated from simulations at higher noise; sampled Clifford-frame trajectories do not prove accessibility for every possible trajectory. The 63.3% branch uses heuristic classical recovery, while the 40.7% branch assumes a search covering the omitted 48-bit ambiguity. The runtime reported here excludes that classical recovery time.

Where further optimization could matter

Two accounting choices identify useful next calculations. The estimate charges every measurement the same duration and treats all memory blocks as occupied throughout. Operation-specific timing and actual memory lifetimes could sharpen the result. Applying the same compiler and direct CCZ construction to another algorithm would also reveal how much benefit depends on this circuit's serial structure.

Per attempt is not time to success

A single attempt may fail, so its duration differs from the time required to obtain a correct answer. If attempts are independent, success has probability \(s\), reset time is negligible, and answers can be checked classically, then \[\Pr(\text{success by attempt }m)=1-(1-s)^m,\qquad \mathbb E[T_{\rm first}]=T/s.\]

Using \(T=25.690\) days and the rounded heuristic \(s=0.633\) gives about 40.6 quantum-compute days to the first success on average. Using \(s=0.407\) gives about 63.1 days. These are derived repeated-attempt expectations under the assumptions above, rather than additional durations claimed for one run.

body:
Symbols and their roles

Symbols acquire their meaning in the lesson where they first enter. This reference collects those meanings so a deep-linked calculation can be read without searching another section.

[[notation]]

Circuit and measurement conventions

The circuits run from left to right. A wire carrying an integer represents a register; a curve-point wire contains its coordinate registers. Filled dots control the connected operation, circled plus signs apply X, and dashed paths carry classical measurement results. An arithmetic box names a subroutine whose internal gates are explained in its lesson.

A Pauli measurement reports bit \(m\) for eigenvalue \((-1)^m\). Measuring X is equivalent to applying a Hadamard and measuring Z. A correction raised to \(m\) is applied for result 1. A zero-initialized wire is clean workspace, and clearing it afterward requires reversible uncomputation or measurement with the corresponding phase repair.
